utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall continue with the evidence of Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two matters while the witness is coming in. P1990 was an exhibit when Mr. Ackerman was cross-examining the witness yesterday. It became apparent that one line apparently was a bad translation, that has been submitted. We do have a new translation, it's been uploaded in e-court, and we seek leave to replace the previous translation with this new one. And P2157 was used by Mr. Ivetic. We had no translation at that time. We since have obtained one and uploaded it into e-court and we would like to advise you of that. We have advised the parties of that and I understand no one has an objection to either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, on the understanding that there's no opposition to the substitution of the new translation of P1990 and to the translation of P2157 being uploaded and admitted as the respective translations of these exhibits, then we shall authorise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic. The first item I want to ask you about is an exhibit I think Mr. Ackerman showed you, it's 6D130. I don't know if you have that in your binder or not. It's a document dated the 27th of March, 1999. Do you recall seeing this one before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's from the assistant to the minister a Major-General Stojan Misic to the -- all the SUPs, to the border police stations, and to the MUP staff head, and to other administrations. I'm interested in item number 1, and it's -- this is in connection with a decision of the federal government to proclaim a state of war. Item 1 says: "Update the list of foreigners." Well, there's a question about the translation. Maybe you should read it out for us and we'll get a translation from the booth as we go. Could you do that? Would you read number 1 for me, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1 reads: "Update the lists of foreigners, those permanently resident and those temporarily residing in the country, as -- and carry out any other preparations for them to perhaps be taken by force to the state border and expelled from the FRY, or rather, taken to whichever reception centres will be designated for this purpose." I'm not sure whether I've read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of this instruction, to update the lists so that they could -- so that the foreigners could be forcibly escorted to the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. I wasn't aware of it at the time. As I told you, I only saw this document during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time of a provision in the law for forcibly removing all foreigners during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of such a provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware now whether there is or was such a provision?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know what law this sort of provision might be part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't know if you've read the document, but it doesn't appear that there's any reference to the law under which that would arise; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. This item does not refer to any specific regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday I think there was a discussion with you about identity cards and passports and documents. I was a little unclear on parts of that discussion. You mentioned that for personal identity cards and passports and other documents there are registers that are kept. Now, can you explain to me where these registers are kept? Are they in the local SUPs or is there some other office where those records were maintained in 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every year the same situation applied. The registers were kept in the secretariat of the interior, and the secretariat of the interior actually issued those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I wasn't clear, were those electronic registers or are there hard copies or both?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of travel documents there were manual registers. I can't remember what the first year was for this sort of procedure to be introduced, but I think one part of the secretariat as from one point in time on, it became electronic. As for personal ID this is done by hand but then all this information is then entered into a unified information system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that if you have the first and last names of each and every person or the citizen's identification number, you can run and check and you can see where and when they were issued with a personal identification document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you said in that answer regarding the personal IDs, this was done by hand and then all this information is entered into a unified information system. Is the unified information system an electronic computer system?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a computer system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have one extra remark to make here. Depending on the equipment that a particular secretariat had available to it, there was some secretariats where the ID documents were typewritten and there were other secretariats where these documents were produced by using a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Bonomy asked you a question yesterday at page 4, line 12, and it was in connection with the answer you gave about -- you said you think that you had heard at the administration that these records were handed over to UNMIK. And Judge Bonomy asked you: What is the source of your information on this? And you said: "In contacts with employees of the administration." My question to you is: Can you name the administration employees from whom you heard that these records had been handed over to UNMIK? Who told you that, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall right now who it was specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say those records were handed over, do you mean the hard copies or electronic files?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how they were handed over. Maybe this was information that was shared on an informal basis and maybe it's something that didn't concern me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know or -- strike that. Even if those documents were handed over to UNMIK, wouldn't the MUP or wouldn't the administration have kept at least a copy for themselves as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how this went and what exactly was handed over. I told you about the types of records that were kept. In my opinion, even if all those registers had been handed over it would have still been down to the unified database of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia to keep all this information, to preserve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Judge Chowhan asked you a question yesterday at page 10 about whether the registers have a column mentioning the ethnicity of a person or whether that information is on or in the ID cards. You said: "Wherever there was a request for personal identification documents to be issued, there was a box that stated the person's ethnicity but no citizen was under an obligation to have that recorded." You went on to say that: "Normally this type of information was something you could always find in the records." How was it that this could always be found in the records? Is it something that's noted on the birth certificates, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this wasn't something that was noted on the birth certificates. The only thing noted at the time was date and place of birth and information regarding parents as well as citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the -- for example, if the individual requesting an identification card did not provide that information, would the governmental clerk or person filling out the form put in ethnicity based on what they observed from the individual, based on their name, based on the language they used?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our country all the forms are filled out by whoever is putting in a request. Every time a form is filled in, the person making the request does it, and then the request is signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If there's no request from the citizen to include their ethnicity on those forms, though, is it left blank?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've seen some records from census I think from 1981 and then we've seen some estimates of the population and the ethnic breakdown in Kosovo for 1991 and later. From where would that information be obtained that showed in some of those reports that the ethnic background of the population of Kosovo was 80 per cent or higher of Albanians? Where is that ethnic information obtained from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume this would have been based on a census. Whenever there is a census, ethnicity is something that is declared by each of the citizens involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are they required to report an ethnicity when the census is taken?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not strictly required as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in 1988 and 1989 in Kosovo you could generally make a good educated guess about somebody's ethnicity simply based on their name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why we should talk about this in reference to 1988 and 1989. It's a generally known fact that members of the Albanian ethnic minority have different names as opposed to Serbs, and the same thing applies in Vojvodina where there is a far greater number of ethnic minorities, the Hungarians, the Ruthinians, the Slovaks and so on and so forth. Therefore, if you look at a person's name, yes, it might make it possible for you to infer their ethnicity, but each person is perfectly free to declare their ethnicity on whatever basis they like. They can say whatever they like. In the former SFRY there were citizens who at a census declared their ethnicity to be Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've seen and heard from some of those. And I apologise, I said 1988 and 1989, I meant 1998 and 1999, but I understand your answer doesn't need to be limited to those years. You talked about where you were housed when you were working for the staff, for the MUP staff in Kosovo, and at page 18, line 21, you told us Novica Zdravkovic sat in one office, your office was opposite his, next to yours was Desimir Slovic, right next to your offices was a big one with Dusko Adamovic and Goran Radosavljevic, and then Mr. Mijatovic and Mr. Lukic had their offices. By my count you only named seven individuals. Was that the total make-up of the MUP staff, just you seven persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people that I met every day and they had each their own office. I forgot to mention General Stojanovic. I can't remember specifically when he first arrived, but he too had an office that was adjacent to Mr. Zdravkovic's office. Those were the people I used to see in those rooms and offices, and I was not really aware of anyone else having an office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're recorded as saying General Stojanovic. What name did you mention there? You forgot that -- that you had forgotten to mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. General Momcilo Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did he join the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember exactly, but I know that he was there too, perhaps, roughly speaking, sometime around October or November but I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is he mentioned in any of these decisions, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not that I recall, Your Honour. I was just about to follow up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was his job or role on the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Several times I heard that he went to some meetings about some flats that were being built.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you know that he was a member of the staff? Did anyone introduce him as that or circulate a memo saying, Welcome General Stojanovic, our new staff member? How did you know that he was part of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say he was part of the staff. All I said was he was there too. He had an office that was next to ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my question was: Was it only seven of you who were on the MUP staff? And then I understood by mentioning him in your answer you were telling us that he was also on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would have to intervene at this point. The witness yesterday mentioned also members who were employed by the Pristina SUP at the same time, so these seven and some other people who were at the same building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is we can't go back on the transcript at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In my question when I asked him about the offices, I asked him specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, what was your point? THE LUKIC: This witness mentioned seven people as members of staff sitting at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there were I think two or three other members of staff who were members of Pristina SUP at the same time, part-time members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that would suggest that the reason for mentioning Stojanovic is connected with the work of the staff, and that's what Mr. Hannis is pursuing. Whether full time or part time, no doubt he's hoping the witness will be able to amplify our knowledge on the matter, that's all. So please -- I think bearing in mind what Mr. Lukic has said, Mr. Hannis, nevertheless it is I think a matter on which we would like a little more information if you can obtain it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, what I am trying to find out is how many MUP staff members were there. You named those seven, including yourself, and General Lukic. Who else was on the MUP staff with you, anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say based on who was there, Mr. Mijatovic, Mr. Dusko Adamovic, Mr. Desimir Slovic, and Mr. Goran Radosavljevic. As for employees of the Ministry of the Interior, those were the ones who had been dispatched to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You just now didn't mention Novica Zdravkovic. Was he or was he not a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novica Zdravkovic was a member of the staff when I first arrived in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that it? Is that the total? Is there anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all. I said yesterday who was there before June 1998, Mr. Djinovic and then he returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, the question that was asked earlier Mr. Hannis said to you: "You told us Zdravkovic sat in one office, your office was opposite his, next to yours was Slovic, right next to your offices was a big one with Adamovic and Radosavljevic, and then Mijatovic and Lukic had their offices. By my count you named only seven. Was that the total make-up of the MUP staff? And you said: "Those were people that I met every day and they had each their own office. I forgot to mention General Stojanovic. I can't remember specifically when he first arrived, but he too had an office that was adjacent to Mr. Zdravkovic's office." Now, so far is that an accurate statement of your position, your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true that I said that, but Mr. Prosecutor asked me about who had their offices there and that is why I said that I just remembered that General Stojanovic's office was right there as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I've just pointed out to you, Mr. Vucurevic, that that was not the question. The question was: "Was that the total make-up of the MUP staff, just you seven persons?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps I misunderstood the question, since we were talking about all the offices that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please help me to understand the position. You've just mentioned as a person who is beside you, in the same working area, at the very least a general called Stojanovic and the only person senior to him working in the office would appear to be General Lukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, General Lukic and General Stojanovic were both major-generals. As I said, I didn't know exactly what General Stojanovic's job was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was suggesting when he interrupted that he was actually a member of the SUP staff who was working part time for the -- sorry, I've misunderstood. What was your point, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were two other members from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. You weren't referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry if I made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm sure it's my misunderstanding. So Stojanovic, can you just tell us one way or another, was he a member of the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I'm only certain about the persons that I have enumerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying that there's a general -- major-general working in there and you don't actually know whether he has any role to play in the staff of which you're part. That is your evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Professionally we were not in touch at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he there very much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he sometimes was. He would come and go. I can't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vucurevic, I'm finding it very difficult to accept that's the sum and substance of your knowledge of the presence of a major-general in an office more or less next to yours during a period of high tension in the most controversial part of the Balkans at that time. Now, please try to help us with a clear indication of the frequency of his attendance there and the general nature of the job he was doing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that I know that he came and that he went to attend some meetings related to housing issues. What it was that he did altogether is something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, he's a police general, not an army general, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police general, yes. And as far as I know he worked at the SUP Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason that I was asking my question was yesterday when you gave us that list of names of people and what offices they were all in, Mr. Lukic went on to ask you: "Apart from these offices, were there any other rooms at the SUP of Pristina that were used by the staff?" Your answer was: "No, we didn't use any other rooms." And then he asked you: "Is that to say that all the members of the staff were present on that same floor in those few offices?" And your answer was: "We were all on the same floor." So is that correct, all you members of the staff were on that same floor and all you members are just those seven persons that you named? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But on that floor where we were there were the offices of the Pristina SUP. There were other employees there as well. I cannot remember now what organizational units they belonged to. I just said that the staff did not have a separate building, separate premises where they were put up. They were put up at the Pristina SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right now I'm not interested in who else might have been on the floor with you. My question is: Is that the total membership of the staff, of the MUP staff, is that you seven guys that you named on that floor and nobody else? I don't care about people from the SUP. I just want to know about the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the persons that I mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about a document, I think it was P1990, and there was a discussion about a plan of the public security sector with a view to preventing and disabling the entry of the military forces of NATO into our territory. And Mr. Lukic asked you: The public -- or maybe it was Mr. Ackerman at this point. You were asked: "The public security sector, is it in charge of defending the state border?" Your answer was: "As far as I know, the public security sector is not in charge of defending the state border." But my question is: But wasn't MUP supposed to work together with the VJ in preventing any possible land invasion by NATO? That was part of the overall defence plan, wasn't it, for MUP to assist VJ in preventing a NATO invasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the defence of the country as far as I know is the task of the Army of Yugoslavia, while the Ministry of the Interior is supposed to take care of its own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during a state of war would not that work include helping prevent an invasion by NATO or do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I asked you a little bit yesterday about the Joint Command, and I think you told us that you maybe heard it one time and we decided that might have been the time when President Milutinovic visited and spoke and mentioned the term. Mr. Ackerman asked you at page 30, line 18, he pointed out to you that one of the things that he and you both know about large organizations is, like police and military, it's all about reporting and paperwork and there's a lot of it. And your answer was: "That's right, but everyone knew only about what they were doing for security reasons." Now, Mr. Vucurevic, that's a concept I'm familiar with in my system and we use the term "need to know." Are you familiar with that term in the context of security concerns, need to know, meaning you're only told what you need to know and nothing more? Is that a concept that you're familiar with in your work?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you put a more specific question. I didn't quite understand. It was a long introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, for example, if I'm General Lukic and I'm going to Joint Command meetings, I may not tell you about it because you don't need to know about the Joint Command to do your job. So do you understand the term "need to know" in that context?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understood. I've already said that General Lukic did not submit reports to me as to what meetings he attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that that may be a reason that you don't know anything about the Joint Command because it's not something that would impact on your work? You told us you didn't deal with the combat operations or the PJP and the SAJ and the work they were doing, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but that's a compound question so I'm not sure what question the witness is actually answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's an appropriate objection, Your Honour. I can go back and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- ask two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, you just said that's possible, are you referring to -- well, let me ask it this way. First of all, you didn't deal with combat operations or what the PJP and the SAJ were doing out in the field in joint operations with the VJ, for example. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so if that were a matter that may have been one of the concerns of a body called the Joint Command, then that could be a reason that you didn't know about the Joint Command because you had nothing to do with those kinds of actions or operations. Do you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I do remember roughly when it was that I heard that term; however, in terms of experience, had this kind of a body existed, just as I said when I heard of a plan, I mean if there was a Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, I would have had to hear about it and know who the members were at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, are you saying it's your position that there was no Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you seem to say that if there had been you must have heard about it or you would have heard about it. Isn't that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said that I heard of the term, as I've said, I heard of a plan and this plan had some stages. So I assume that I would have to have at least some basic knowledge of the existence of something and where that something was, although I did not deal with that and that was not part of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In your preparations for testifying, were you shown a document, it's our Exhibit Number P2166, which are the minutes of a meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff for combatting terrorism in Kosovo. It's a meeting that included Mr. Milosevic, President Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, General Lukic, General Pavkovic, and several other members of the higher-ranking officials of the army, the MUP, and the political personnel. Do you recall being shown that document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see in that that Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, President Milosevic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Minic, and your own General Lukic all referred to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija during that meeting. You saw that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I think I did see that when I was looking at documents and I looked at quite a few documents. I cannot remember exactly what is stated in each and every document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you aware that General Lukic has told the investigators of the OTP that he attended meetings of the Joint Command in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's in an exhibit in this trial. Having heard that and having seen that document of the meeting that I asked you about before, does that change your opinion about whether or not there may have been a Joint Command but you just didn't become aware of it when you were in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Never mind. I'll move on to my last question because I've run over my time. I want to show you exhibit P1811. I can hand you a hard copy with the assistance of the usher. Now, I know this is dated after you left Kosovo, because I understand you were injured -- was that on the 1st of April, Mr. Vucurevic, when you were injured in the bombing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 29th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where General Lukic and Colonel Mijatovic were at the time you got injured in that bombing? Were they in the same building?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was injured, they were not in the building of the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document, P1811, is dated the 31st of May, 1999, and you'll see it's a decision on the establishment of the ministry staff for the suppression of terrorism. That's the same title we saw on Exhibit P1505 from June 16th of 1998, right? And if you would look at the last page, page 2 of the English, item number 6, this decision supersedes the decision on the establishment of the ministry staff for the suppression of terrorism, number 1580/98 of 16 June 1998, which I will tell you is at Exhibit P1505. So other than this document and P1505 for the period from June 1998 to May 31st, 1999, it appears there was no other document in force regarding the ministry staff for the suppression of terrorism. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do agree because what is written here is that this decision is no longer in force once this decision is adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, you indicated to us that there were occasions when you saw Gajic and you mentioned the lunchroom as a place you would see him within the building. Over what period was it that you were aware of his presence there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly but I think that it was immediately upon arrival. This was a common room where we had breakfast, lunch, and dinner. So all the people who worked in Pristina came there, people who worked in Pristina but had actually come from other secretariats and other organizational units outside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And over what period of time were you aware that he was around?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean for how long he was there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a time after which you just didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, but I think that while I was there he wasn't there all the time. Now, was this in the autumn of 1998? As far as I know, by then he was no longer in Pristina. I didn't see him then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So after what time? Can you help me? After what date roughly did you not see him again?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've said, I cannot remember exactly. I think it was either September or October. I'm not quite sure, because I didn't see all these people every day. Sometimes you would see someone and sometimes you simply wouldn't run into them. I just know that he worked at the state security sector and that he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw Legija on one occasion. Do you remember roughly when that was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I truly cannot remember. I just know that I saw him once during lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember the day that General Lukic first arrived to take up his position as head of the staff? I don't mean the date. Can you remember him arriving to take up his post?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that day, of course. I cannot remember the exact date, but a meeting was held and I think that the previous head of staff was there, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Novica Zdravkovic, Mr. Goran Radosavljevic, then Mr. Miodrag Zumovic [phoen], and I. I don't think I can remember anybody else being present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was to happen to the previous head?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he went back to the job he held before that at the traffic police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So did you find out why Mr. Lukic was there, why he had been appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood things, the previous head of staff had already spent a year in Pristina. It was my understanding that that is why he was going back to his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me in maybe two or three sentences what was the purpose of the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I really didn't understand what the point of this staff was either. I can say briefly what I know of, that is to say what I know of what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything that you did that couldn't have been done by using the ordinary organizational units of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for my line of work, I didn't do anything that they couldn't have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a bit of a puzzle then what this body was there for as far -- in your mind at least.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said when I went to the administration once or twice for preparations, that nobody showed me what it was that this staff did nor did anyone tell me clearly, precisely, and concisely, these are your obligations, these are your powers, this is what you're supposed to do. I told you what the circumstances were surrounding my secondment to Pristina. It was my understanding that it was some kind of a punishment. It's not that I was promoted, that I was sent to a higher position. They sent me to Kosovo in the period when practically every day a policeman or a citizen would get killed or abducted. So I went there highly dissatisfied, and I didn't have any choice. I only could have resigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you never got the impression while you were there that there was a need in dealing with the Kosovo problem for a body that would coordinate the activity of the police, the various police organizational units within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not the impression I had. I am speaking from the vantage point of the line of work that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything arising from that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Re-examination, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is coming to an end, isn't it. I asked you something on Friday, page 23055. That question was not recorded, it just says "the 16th of June, 1998," that will probably be corrected. However, in your answer you say from line 17 onwards, I'm going to read it out in English so that you would receive a proper interpretation of the English transcript. [In English] "Also, there were persons there who were working at the Pristina SUP, such as Milorad Rajicic, Rasko Milenkovic, and Dr. Dobrasin Krdzic and Milutin Vukovic. I think that he also worked in the Pristina SUP." [Interpretation] Out of these persons you mentioned here, can you remember who it was that worked at the Pristina SUP while simultaneously carrying out duties in the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Mr. Rajicic, then Mr. Krdzic, then -- no, I forgot the last name and when I was speaking then I had the document in front of me. The man who was an analyst and I'm sure that he worked at the SUP Pristina. I just wasn't sure about Vukovic, whether he worked at the Pristina SUP then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us then look at P1505.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Rasko Milenkovic is the name that slipped my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were these persons members of the staff to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the staff, that is how they were introduced to me too and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they sit with you on the same floor in those six or seven offices?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they used their regular offices, their regular work premises in the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These offices of theirs, were they in the same building or in different buildings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said there was several buildings in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But were they part of the same complex of buildings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milorad Rajicic had an office one or two floors above mine, so I know for sure that he was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today on page 5, line 24, you were asked whether ethnicity was recorded in the card required for issuing a personal identity card. Do you remember there was an explicit remark on that card that the applicant was under no obligation to state his or her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot now remember the exact contents of that application form, but I do know that the officials at the window have no right to ask an applicant to state their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up 6D269.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Ackerman asked you yesterday why the addressee, state security sector, has a remark, for their information, next to it. First we have to see who signed this document and their official title.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief of sector, Lieutenant-General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for him to order anything to the state security sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he cannot order anything to the state security sector because the latter has it own chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With this same document you were asked to look at item 7, referring to volunteer and paramilitary units and their members. For as long as you were in Kosovo and Metohija, did you know whether there were any volunteers on the police force?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shown document P1989. We don't need it on the screen, but on page 2 you were shown a report from the chief of secretariat in Gnjilane, Colonel Dusan Gavranic, where he says that there had been problems with volunteers in Zegra. I will show you 6D614.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it in e-court, please, page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In para 2 what is written?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Village Zegra, 31st March 1999, homicide under Article 47 of the criminal law of the Republic of Serbia. On 31st March 1999 authorised officers with the secretariat in Gnjilane filed a criminal complaint KU number 183/99 against Vlado Zmajevic from Niksic, Zeljko Djuricic from Zrenjanin, Ratko Soldat from Vrbas, Goran Kostelnik from Vrbas, Sasa Djosanovic from Zrenjanin, Nikola Ivelic from Vrbas, and Damir Novic from Zrenjanin. Members of the volunteer unit of the VJ for the criminal act of homicide against Uksin Uksini and Djazim Haziri from Zegra village. The perpetrators were remanded in custody under Article 196 of the Law on Criminal Procedure. The criminal complaint was submitted to the office of the competent military prosecutor on the 1st of April, 1999. An investigation of the crime scene was conducted and photo documentation compiled. The case is under jurisdiction of the competent army authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see from this which volunteers are the subject of this report by the chief of secretariat Dusan Gavranic? Were you aware of this or have you -- did you already leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had already left, but it says here a volunteer unit of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court P1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is the document where I indicated before that we would admit portions of it, and you indicated that there are still translations ongoing in relation to parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On reflection, the best plan I think is to simply mark for identification each passage as it comes and deal with the thing in one all-encompassing order in due course to keep things under control and there will be no doubt in anybody's mind about what has been admitted, rather than that piecemeal suggestion I made. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have one witness at the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- who took part in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's yet another reason why we should leave the final disposition of any part of this until that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of doubt in the transcript, that comment refers to 6D614 and not to the exhibit you're now calling up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, do you have P1990 before you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Ackerman suggested to you that Sreten Lukic was superior to the minister and his two assistants by virtue of the fact that he was chairing this meeting. You explained that the fact was he was like a host at the staff, and I want to ask you: In February 1999 is it the case that Minister Stojiljkovic, Generals Djordjevic and Obradovic [sic], at this moment on the 17th of February, 1999, were permanently in Kosovo and Metohija or did they come as guests on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they had come as guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Sreten Lukic superior at that meeting or at any time in 1998 or 1999 to Minister Stojiljkovic, chief of the state security -- sorry, chief of the public security sector Djordjevic or his assistant Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't superior to them and he couldn't be because they had higher positions, especially Djordjevic, who worked at the SUP in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again for the avoidance of doubt, although I think it becomes clear, your reference was not to General Obradovic, I take it, but to General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake, I wrote it wrong as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you meant Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I meant Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But also we have to correct something in the transcript, line 7, page 28, it says that Djordjevic who worked at the SUP in Belgrade, it was actually Lukic who came to the MUP staff from the SUP Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 28, which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 7 and 8, but I can ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, who came to the MUP staff in Kosovo from SUP Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, General Sreten Lukic and I believe also Mr. Dusko Adamovic had worked in SUP Belgrade and I believe even Goran Radosavljevic worked in SUP Belgrade. Only Mr. Mijatovic had come from the police administration from the headquarters of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up in e-court 6D262.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Hannis asked you how you received the assignments you were to carry out in Kosovo and Metohija. The last paragraph in B/C/S, page 1, reads: "For purposes of uniform treatment of diplomatic and consular missions, representatives of international organizations and international humanitarian organizations accredited in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it is necessary to proceed as follows." And then on the next page we have the procedures listed. My question is: Does this dispatch also stipulate your assignments vis-a-vis diplomats, representatives of humanitarian organizations, and other international organizations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Item by item it is listed here exactly how we were to proceed with representatives of these international organizations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have responsibilities in relation to diplomats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the Prosecution Exhibit P1693.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have it so please look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need only page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's an overview of security-related important events dated 1st May 1999. I would like you to comment on what you see on the last page, namely, that 715.158 persons had left Kosovo, although that's not the time when you were there. But since you were asked about this I want to ask you too. If you don't know, say that you don't know. Did you hear from your colleagues whether these people were counted precisely or was it an estimate of the employees at border crossings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about it, but I think it must be an estimate because with those crowds and pressure at border crossings I believe it's impossible to count and register all those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the possibility that their documents could not be checked, could that be one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be one of the reasons. As far as I know, there was no checking done or recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 6D768.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have that, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you about this document, could you tell us what are instructions, orders in the sense of "nalog" and orders to update?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "nalog" is when somebody's told how to proceed in a particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about updating?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that somebody's reminded of the obligation they were given earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Hannis showed you this document and suggested that Sreten Lukic ordered the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija to do certain things, jobs, which means he issued instructions or orders suggesting that the police was not performing its job professionally. Now, look at item 1, 2, and 3, what exactly this contains. You don't have to read.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this page opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you at least look at 1 and 2? I'll read it for you. "In order to prevent and suppress such occurrences, it is necessary to do the following: "1. Ensure full control over the employees of the ministry every day and demand that they carry out their tasks professionally and responsibly. "2. Vigorously institute criminal misdemeanour and disciplinary proceedings against the perpetrators of such actions proportional to the seriousness and type of act and the manner in which it was carried out. "3. Record any such occurrences and events and report immediately to the ministry staff in Pristina." Are these specific orders in the sense of "nalog" being issued here or is the only thing that's being pointed out the legal obligation that the SUPs have?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what is being pointed out here is the obligation that all members of the secretariat have under the law. I must say again, I wasn't the one who produced this document, but I think it is being highlighted again here to the chiefs because of the situation that prevailed in Kosovo. This type of work needed to be performed on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 3 says: "Record all such instances and immediately report to the ministry staff in Pristina." What we see being emphasised here, is this not something that the SUPs were already doing in relation to the Ministry of the Interior staff, they were reporting, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph on page 2, could you please look at that: "Chiefs in the secretariat and commanders of the PJP joint detachment shall be personally responsible for the implementation of the above measures and for preventing such occurrences." Who would normally have been responsible for carrying out these tasks, or rather, did Sreten Lukic change something around in relation to what would normally have been the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A chief of the secretariat is responsible for the tasks and work of his own secretariat in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 6D798.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These minutes are not complete, and perhaps that's why they were used to explain the substance of the document itself. Let me ask you this: You were at this meeting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that minutes of meetings taken at the MUP staff for as long as you were a member were taken by Slovic, right? Were those meetings tape recorded or video recorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that those meetings were recorded in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Slovic ever made any shorthand notes from these meetings? Was he properly trained to do something like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that he was one of the analysts in that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he simply hand-write whatever was being said at the meeting by just taking handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was actually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My last question, it's about 1D144.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a decree on ID during a state of war. Do you know if these provisions applied to Kosovo and Metohija or did they apply throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applied throughout the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vucurevic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, on cross-examination and re-examination something was raised, of course I'm not entitled to any additional questions but there is a reference there to volunteers based on the MUP report and the evidence that Mr. Lukic has been using. I just want to tell the Chamber that these are volunteers about whom there is already evidence, they were Prosecutor's -- this is 5D825 and 5D955 -- P955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can make these submissions in due course, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence to us. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall now take a break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is Mr. Radojica Nikcevic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikcevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Nikcevic. For purposes of the record, could you please identify yourself.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Radojica Nikcevic. My father's name was Radomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you give us a short biography of yourself, including your educational background.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Pec 1965. I resided both in Pec and in a village between Pec and Decani, it's called Dojca Rena [phoen]. I completed my secondary -- my elementary education in Rausic and my secondary education in Pec and the highest school in Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly tell us about your employment within the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I had been with the MUP since 1991, more specifically I was first deployed to Pec and that went on until 1995. In 1995 I was dispatched to the police department that was attached to the Pec SUP, Celopek. In 2002 I was re-deployed to the gendarmerie department in Belgrade. I am now in a unit that deals with the special action tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I -- am I to understand correctly that you are now an instructor in the unit that deals with special action tactics?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because that didn't make it into the transcript. Now, if we could focus for a moment at the time-period of 1998/1999, what precise posts or positions did you hold in the Serbian MUP at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: An employee of the Pec SUP of the Ministry of the Interior. I am a police member, a policeman. In mid-2002 I joined the PJP. Later on in 1999 I joined the OPG, and in 2002 I joined Belgrade's gendarmerie.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, sir, the transcript records you as saying in mid-2002 you joined the PJP. Is that date accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: It was in June 2002 the PJP, which used to be the PJM and then later the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it 2002 or 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I permutated, I apologise, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your employment within the secretariat of interior in Pec, did you know -- and again focusing on the time-period 1998 to 1999, did you know of any non-Serbs that were employed by the SUP Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were Muslims there, Roma, and a certain number of Albanians or Siptars. More specifically, in the department where I worked in Celopek, working with me was Zenun Gashi, a Roma, and Samija Ademi, a Siptar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've already told us when you became a part of the PJP. Can you tell us the circumstances how you became a part of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the circumstances. I know I passed a test of physical and mental abilities, and I met the requirements because I was a policeman in the Pec SUP. All members of the PJP who were admitted to the Pec PJP took that test and passed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Had you been selected by anyone to become a member of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I had been recommended by my direct superior, the commander of the Pec police station Besavic Dragan or maybe one of the other officers effected that particular selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the OPG, could you tell us what that acronym stands for?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: OPG as such, OPG, it exists, existed, since sometime in the 1970s. The abbreviation stands for operative pursuit group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the particular OPG that you were a part with, what areas provided members for that OPG and what was the total number of persons, the manpower, of that unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, those were men -- not for the most part. For the most part those were men who were from the PJP and then were proposed, their names were put forward for additional training that was done with members of the OPG. And in terms of manpower, the Pec SUP numbered ten men together with Klina and Istok, about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what types of assignments you would undertake as a PJP or OPG member?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the PJP - and the same thing applies to the OPG - since we were within the PJP we worked on the same kinds of assignments. For the most part these had to do with upholding public law and order. To a high extent it was about that. We provided security for various sports -- sporting events. We maintained check-points. Those were our assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The membership of the PJP company in Pec, were those all policemen?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you would not be engaged as part of the PJP or OPG for specific assignments, what jobs did you then undertake when not engaged in the PJP/OPG?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Our regular jobs, mine was with the police department in Celopek and the others worked in the Pec police station, working within the sector, patrolling sector check-points, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was Vidomir Salipur and what eventually happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Vidomir Salipur was a policeman of the Pec police station. He was killed sometime in 1999 on the 8th of April, in the village of Radovac in a vehicle in which he was moving from Pec to Rozaje. He was hit by a hand-held launcher and another member who was in a different vehicle was wounded on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many PJP units were within the SUP Pec? What was the structure?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: The structure was as follows: Two platoons in Pec and one each in Klina and Istok. At the outset, the Djakovica SUP had a platoon which makes up a total of five. Later Djakovica SUP splinted off from the Pec SUP, and instead of the Djakovica platoon, the traffic police platoon was now attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time-periods when you were not called up nor engaged as part of the PJP or OPG, who were your superiors within the SUP Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: My direct superior was Dragan Kerseljevic, the commander of the police station; later on when I moved to the Celopek police department, the police department commander Milos Krstic and his deputy Esad Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now when you were operating as part of the PJP, who were your superior officers at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: At the outset the company commander was Radomir Colic; his deputy, Dragan Kerseljevic; the platoon commander, Dragan Djukic; and the department or squad commander, Miomir Jovanovic. In mid-1998, I mean I would like to say that Dragan Kerseljevic when this was splinted off from the Djakovica and Pec SUP became the company commander. His deputy was Srdjan Perovic. The platoon commander remained the same and Joksovic Sasa now became the squad commander. And when Captain Perovic was killed in Lodza and commander Kerseljevic was wounded and platoon Commander Djukic was killed, some changes were introduced to the command structure. Krsto Djuricic now became company commander, his deputy was Dragan Stojkovic, and the platoon commander was Vidomir Salipur.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you operated as part of the OPG, who were your superior officers at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was the company commander at that time, Djuricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what differences were there between the PJP and the OPG?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see any difference between these two formations except that the OPG had somewhat more training than the members of the PJP. Also, there was specialised training in the OPG. Just one more thing, if I may change something. Here I said Stojkovic Dragan I think previously, and it's not Dragan, it's Nenad Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the PJP and the OPG are concerned, was there any difference in pay between those that were just PJP and those that were PJP as well as OPG?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was no difference. Everything was the same except, as I've said, the difference is that members of the OPG underwent more training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the numerical strength was of your PJP company?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Around 80 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you remember, in 1999 what radio call-signs did the PJP from Pec utilise?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Call-signs, as for where I was, the 1st Platoon, it was Grom; for the 5th Platoon, I mean this other one that was there in the SUP of Pec was mine. When the platoon commander Djukic got killed, the call-sign Grom was one that we no longer used. Then the entire group of the 1st and 5th Platoon took over the call-sign Munja.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is possibly what the speaker said a few moments ago but we did not hear him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess with the interpreter's comments I should ask the witness to repeat the call-signs sitting closer to the microphone. Could you re --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before -- yeah, you better do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat what both call-signs were that you mentioned a few moments ago in answering my question, as the interpreters did not catch the -- just repeat the two call-signs that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: The call-sign was Grom and there was the call-sign Munja.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us something about the training that you underwent when you became a member of the OPG?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember every detail of what it was that we went through during training, but training was primarily psychological and physical resilience, tactics, we also had target practice. That would be about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where that training for the OPG took place.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: At Mount Goc.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for those of us that are not familiar with the geography, could you tell us, is Goc within or outside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Goc is near Kraljevo, outside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who else was in your training group, what SUPs were represented at this training at the Goc mountain?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that at the time when I was there for training in the month of December 1998 that the other members were from the territory of Kosovo, that is to say the SUPs from Kosovo, Pristina, Mitrovica, Gnjilane, Urosevac, Prizren, Djakovica, and Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell us who led the training for -- the training at this facility at Goc?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Goran Radosavljevic led the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us if you remember who some of the other instructors were for this OPG training that you underwent?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: The instructors were from the MUP. I didn't know them. We addressed them as Mr. Instructor. I know after we got out I got to know Radomir Djeric, who I saw at the gendarmerie, he was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall some of the specific themes that were covered as part of the training course?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was reconnaissance and observation, movement on the ground, using tear gas, break and entry into premises, placing check-points, or rather, barriers to stop vehicles and persons on a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any theoretical courses also covered as part of the training?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before we would do practical work, the theoretical part would be presented to us as to what it was we were doing, what the subject was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now, could you tell us upon completion of your OPG training what did you do immediately upon returning from this training?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Regular work at the police station, or rather, I was attached or returned to the Celopek police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, focusing on the policemen of the SUP Pec, what were the types of fire-arms issued to all policemen and what different fire-arms were there for members of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Policemen were personally issued with a pistol CZ-99 and an automatic rifle respectively, M70 AB2. The same -- or actually, as members of the police we had TT's. First it was the members of the PJP that got CZ-99s and then subsequently other members of the SUPs replaced their pistols, their TT pistols, with the CZ-99.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any additional fire-arms or weapons that were available to the PJ -- to the police officers who were called up as part of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Individuals were issued with something, or rather, the company was issued with a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a PHT, 7.62-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you make a reference to a particular type of sniper rifle? The interpreters state that they did not hear the reference after sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: A classical rifle that was used in the army and police in the then-Yugoslavia, present-day Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What uniforms were worn by the police of the SUP in Pec in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Policemen wore regular uniforms, that is to say a blue jacket, navy blue, dark blue; then a light blue shirt with epaulettes; trousers that were navy blue; shoes; and a black leather belt with additional attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what uniforms did the members of the PJP wear?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Members of the PJP wore multi-coloured navy blue jackets, shirts, trousers, and boots on their feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during what time-period was that uniform of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the period is mid-1998, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how did the PJP uniform change at that point in time? What was the new PJP uniform?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Olive-green-grey, green, the same thing as a set except that it was olive-green-grey, and also I added there was a belt with accessories, with an extension.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any emblems or insignia on the PJP uniform?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the sleeve we would have a shield with the tri-colour flag and letters saying the police. That's on the left sleeve. On the right sleeve PJP insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to wear any vests; and if so, how were those marked?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: Vests were used in action, they were also olive-green-grey. On the back it said "police" and on the front on the right-hand pocket. Also there were accessories on them for the necessary equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could tell us how visible were these markings, that is to say from how far away approximately could they be noted and distinguished?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: It depended on whether it was day-time or night-time. In day-time the visibility was 100 metres because the letters were white, so it was noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did any members of your PJP unit wear any non-standard uniforms different from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: No. The principle of uniformity was highly respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to wear ribbons on the uniforms; and if so, what was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that we wore ribbons twice, once -- I mean in two periods. After Perovic was caught in July, Captain Perovic, in Lodza, the terrorists wore police uniforms and that's how they tricked him and arrested him. From then onwards I know that we wore ribbons. I think -- well, it's not that I think, it's the way it should be. They were white, yellow, and red.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us in what --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: And in the second period --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Wait a second, please. First of all, dealing with the first period that you've just described after Perovic was caught in July. What year was that during?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: 1998, the month of July, the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you go on to the second time-period when ribbons were used along with the uniforms. When was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA NIKCEVIC
utterances.text: I know that the action was in Rugova, that's when we wore them, that is to say around the 15th, around the 15th.
